c.tagline: Rock Islands rise from turquoise lagoons around a diver's paradise.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are officially required but rarely used; agree on a flat fare (typically $6-10 in town) with the driver before departing.

emergency.note: 911 reaches police/fire/ambulance dispatch nationwide; response times can be slow outside central Koror.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The compact commercial core along Main Street with WCTC department store, restaurants, dive shops and banks; best for first-timers who want everything walkable and no car needed.
Palau's marina and scuba-diving hub, ringed by dive operators, boat docks and over-water lodging; ideal for divers and snorkelers heading out early to the Rock Islands.
A quieter, greener peninsula across a short causeway from downtown, anchored by the island's premier beachfront resort; suits travelers wanting resort comfort at a slower pace.
On Babeldaob just across the Japan-Palau Friendship Bridge near the airport, with larger resort-style pools and easy late-arrival/early-departure access; suits fly-in-fly-out travelers.
Residential hillside hamlets with mangrove channel views, small B&Bs and dive-guide-run homestays; suits budget travelers and those wanting an authentic local stay.
lodging: West Plaza Hotel by the Sea

water.note: Central Koror's tap water is treated and generally considered safe, though sensitive travelers may prefer bottled water.

transit.pay: There is no fare-card system; shuttle and taxi fares are paid directly to the driver in cash. Resort shuttle passes are sometimes sold as weekly ride books (around $7) through hotels.
transit.hours: Resort shuttle vans typically run roughly 5PM-10PM connecting hotels to downtown; daytime and late-night public transit is minimal.
transit.note: Koror has no fixed-route public bus system for general use; most visitors rely on rental cars, hotel shuttles, the Grab app, or negotiated taxis.

bus: Hotel/resort shuttle vans (BBI and similar operators)
ferry: Ferries to Peleliu and Angaur states
Rock Islands tour boats from Malakal

tip.r: Not traditionally expected in Palauan culture, but small tips are increasingly appreciated at tourist-oriented restaurants, dive shops and resorts.

food.name: Fruit Bat Soup
food.desc: Palau's most notorious dish: a whole fruit bat simmered in coconut milk with ginger and root vegetables, served fur, wings and all.

places.name: Carp Restaurant
places.note: The long-established address for the classic whole-bat version; order ahead.

places.name: Kramers Cafe
places.note: Waterside deck kitchen that cooks bat soup and other traditional Palauan plates.

places.name: Emaimelei Restaurant
places.note: Family-run local kitchen for Palauan specialities away from the tourist menus.

food.name: Demok (Taro Leaf and Coconut Stew)
food.desc: Taro leaves slow-cooked to a thick green stew with coconut milk and often crab or clam meat; eaten with boiled taro corm rather than rice.

places.name: Bem Ermii
places.note: Local favourite specialising in everyday Palauan dishes, demok included.

places.name: Koror Public Market
places.note: Stalls sell taro, taro leaf and cooked demok in takeaway tubs each morning.

places.name: Carp Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Palauan menu with taro dishes served alongside the seafood.

food.name: Tuna Sashimi
food.desc: Yellowfin landed the same morning and cut thick; Japanese-era influence meets Palau's tuna grounds, usually with soy, wasabi and lime.

places.name: Mog Mog Sushi
places.note: Small sushi counter locals rate for the freshness of the day's tuna.

places.name: Drop Off Bar and Grill
places.note: Diver hangout serving big sashimi plates with harbour views.

places.name: Elilai Seaside Restaurant
places.note: Travellers' Choice sunset restaurant plating sashimi Pacific Rim style.

food.name: Ulkoy (Pumpkin Fritters)
food.desc: Shredded pumpkin, sometimes with shrimp, bound in batter and deep fried into crisp golden patties; Palau's favourite snack and party food.

places.name: Koror Public Market
places.note: Fritters and taro chips sold warm from market and roadside stalls.

places.name: Bem Ermii
places.note: Reliable spot for ulkoy and other fried Palauan snacks by the plate.

places.name: Kramers Cafe
places.note: Serves ulkoy as a starter beside its seafood mains.

food.name: Mangrove Crab in Coconut Milk
food.desc: Chesbreng, the fat mangrove crab of Palau's tidal forests, steamed or stewed in coconut milk; a feast dish reserved for special occasions.

places.name: Carp Restaurant
places.note: Known for mangrove crab cooked the traditional way; call ahead in season.

places.name: Elilai Seaside Restaurant
places.note: Refined crab dishes with Rock Islands sunset views.

places.name: Drop Off Bar and Grill
places.note: Casual harbourside plates of local crab and reef fish.

food.name: Palauan Plate Lunch
food.desc: The working lunch: fried or grilled reef fish with rice, boiled taro or tapioca and a scoop of coconut greens, packed in a styrofoam box.

places.name: Koror Public Market
places.note: Cheapest and most authentic takeaway lunches on the island.

places.name: Emaimelei Restaurant
places.note: Home-style Palauan cooking at local, not resort, prices.

places.name: WCTC Shopping Center food counters
places.note: Deli counters where office workers grab hot plate lunches.

food.name: Young Coconut Water
food.desc: Green drinking coconuts opened with a machete; the everyday thirst-quencher in a hot, humid archipelago where they grow on every shoreline.

places.name: Koror Public Market
places.note: Fresh coconuts and cut fruit sold every morning.

places.name: Rock Islands tour boats
places.note: Coconuts are a standard part of the beach lunch on day trips.

places.name: Roadside stalls, Koror-Airai Road
places.note: Family stands selling coconuts and bananas along the causeway road.

food.name: Red Rooster Beer
food.desc: Palau's own craft lager and pale ale, brewed in Koror by the Palau Brewing Company; the standard order after a day in the water.

places.name: Red Rooster Brewery and Taproom
places.note: Palau Brewing Company's own bar, freshest pours on the island.

places.name: Drop Off Bar and Grill
places.note: Dive-crew bar where the local beer is on tap after boats come in.

places.name: Kramers Cafe
places.note: Waterside deck for a cold local beer at sunset.

train.note: Palau has no railways. Arrive by air into Roman Tmetuchl International Airport near Koror, with flights from Manila, Taipei, Seoul and Guam. There is no rail anywhere in Micronesia.

bus.note: No international coaches. Palau has no real public bus system - a shuttle runs between the main Koror hotels and shopping areas, and most visitors use taxis, hire cars or dive-shop transfers. The road bridge links Koror with Babeldaob and the airport.

intl.to: Peleliu & Angaur (Palau) - state boats, a few days a week
intl.op: Palau state ferry operators — tickets at the Koror dock

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry - all arrivals are by air. The state boats to Peleliu and Angaur run only a couple of times a week and are weather-dependent, so most visitors reach the southern islands by chartered speedboat or dive boat. The Rock Islands, Palau's main attraction, are visited on permit-only day trips by boat.
